question: Are NYC's streets more dangerous at night? Make a chart and give a conclusion for a news report.

options.metric: Share of reported crashes involving at least one person injured or killed: crashes with (number_of_persons_injured > 0 or number_of_persons_killed > 0) divided by all eligible crashes in the same time group
options.denominator: Eligible crashes in the same time group
options.grouping: Day: 06:00–19:59; night: 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59; exact 00:00 is a separate possible-default-time group
options.reason: A crash-level injury/fatal involvement share directly compares how often reported crashes at night versus daytime involved harm without implying a traffic exposure denominator.
options.answer: In complete 2013–2025 records, 28.6% of night crashes involved injury or death versus 23.4% of daytime crashes; the separate 00:00 group was 26.7%.
options.interpretation: This framing compares the share of one-row-per-crash police reports from complete calendar years 2013–2025 with at least one reported person injured or killed, using crashes with known time and both outcome fields as the denominator; day is 06:00–19:59, night is 20:00–23:59 plus 00:01–05:59, and exact 00:00 is separate. The share is 28.6% for 500,924 night crashes, 23.4% for 1,607,466 daytime crashes, and 26.7% for 23,786 eligible exact-midnight crashes. This is a defensible comparison of how often reported crashes involve harm, but it cannot establish per-trip or per-mile danger because the data have no traffic-exposure denominator. The check found partial 2012 (July 1–December 31) and 2026 (January 1–June 11), which were excluded; 42 of 2,132,218 complete-year records (0.002%) were missing one or both injury/death fields and were excluded, and of 23,787 exact-00:00 records (1.12%), 23,786 eligible rows were kept separately while one missing-outcome row was excluded; no dates or times were missing.

options.metric: Mean reported casualties per crash, calculated as the sum of number_of_persons_injured plus number_of_persons_killed divided by eligible crashes in the same time group
options.denominator: Eligible crashes in the same time group
options.grouping: Day: 06:00–19:59; night: 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59; exact 00:00 is a separate possible-default-time group
options.reason: Average casualties per crash captures the reported injury-and-death burden of crashes rather than only whether a crash had any casualties.
options.answer: Night crashes averaged 0.409 reported injured or killed people per crash, compared with 0.310 for daytime crashes; the separate 00:00 group averaged 0.359.
options.interpretation: This framing compares mean casualties—reported persons injured plus killed divided by crashes with known time and both outcome fields—in one-row-per-crash police reports from complete calendar years 2013–2025; day is 06:00–19:59, night is 20:00–23:59 plus 00:01–05:59, and exact 00:00 is separate. Mean casualties per crash are 0.409 for 500,924 night crashes, 0.310 for 1,607,466 daytime crashes, and 0.359 for 23,786 eligible exact-midnight crashes. This is a defensible comparison of the reported harm burden per crash, but it cannot establish per-trip or per-mile danger because traffic exposure is not in the data. The check found partial 2012 (July 1–December 31) and 2026 (January 1–June 11), which were excluded; 42 of 2,132,218 complete-year records (0.002%) were missing one or both injury/death fields and were excluded, and of 23,787 exact-00:00 records (1.12%), 23,786 eligible rows were kept separately while one missing-outcome row was excluded; no dates or times were missing.

answer:
In complete 2013–2025 records, 28.6% of reported night crashes involved injury or death, versus 23.4% of daytime crashes (the separate 00:00 group was 26.7%); this compares reported crashes, not exposure-adjusted street risk.
Night crashes averaged 0.409 reported injured or killed people per crash, versus 0.310 by day (the separate 00:00 group averaged 0.359), but this does not establish higher per-trip or per-mile danger.
